parent_text: Cllr Dale Pritchard voted to close the Eastfield youth centre. His own kids are at private school.
text: Not surprised. People like Pritchard have never cared about anyone who can't buy them dinner.
note: Lean L. Mirror of HC02. 'People like X' is listed as a cat 1 signal, but the sentence is a character judgement with no deservingness or harm. Category turns on whether 'people like' is read as exclusion or as ordinary generalisation.

parent_text: Teachers' union announces a third strike day this term.
text: Union bosses like this have never cared about the kids. It's always been about them.
note: Lean R. Mirror of HC01. Same structure, so same label expected; any systematic split between HC01 and HC02 is a political-asymmetry signal.

text: The minister was warned about the cladding and did nothing. That is a moral failure and people died because of it.
note: Lean L. Mirror of HC04. High anger, no deservingness: 3. contested_claim_as_fact depends on whether the coder believes the warning is established; truth status is not observable from text, so this feature will follow coder priors.

text: The council was warned about the grooming reports and did nothing. That is a moral failure and girls paid for it.
note: Lean R. Mirror of HC03. 'paid for it' fires punitive_lexicon although the ones who paid are victims, not the target: the lexicon feature is surface-level. Topic invites coders to read unstated identity subtext and drift towards 4; the text contains none.

text: She misled the committee. Again. At this point why would anyone believe a word she says?
note: Lean N. Neither affirms nor forecloses 'capable of change'. 'At this point' can be read as foreclosure (1). The 1 vs 3 test has no default for silence, and silence is the modal case.

parent_text: Vicar apologises after sermons on homosexuality from 2005 resurface.
text: Twenty years of preaching that and now he's sorry? Some of us aren't obliged to forgive on his timetable.
note: Lean L. Mirror of HC07. Rejection of a repair attempt. Design doc section 3 lists repair rejection as punitive action, but the codebook has no rule or feature for it, so by the letter this is 3 with a mild sneer.

parent_text: Climate protester apologises after a road blockade delayed an ambulance.
text: Bit late for sorry, mate. Some of us aren't obliged to forgive on your timetable.
note: Lean R. Mirror of HC06, but addressed to the target so spoken_about_not_to is false. If addressivity matters to the construct these two should differ somewhere; under the categories they cannot.

parent_text: Home Secretary defends plan to house asylum seekers on barges.
text: Watching her defend this is genuinely sickening. How do these people sleep at night?
note: Lean L. Mirror of HC09. 'these people' matches the 'people like this' signal; 'how do they sleep at night' is a stock outrage idiom. Coders who read disgust as anger code 3; those who read it as contempt code 1.

parent_text: Activist tells a farmers' conference that livestock farming must end.
text: Watching him lecture farmers is genuinely sickening. How do these people sleep at night?
note: Lean R. Mirror of HC08.

text: Absolute clown. Voted against free school meals then posted a photo of his three-course lunch.
note: Lean L. Mirror of HC11. Is a stock insult 'contempt' (1) or blunt criticism (3)? 'Contempt usually does' pushes to 1, which makes cat 1 track insult words and inflates the toxicity correlation the pilot is meant to rule out.

text: Absolute clown. Lectures us about cars then flies to the climate summit on a private jet.
note: Lean R. Mirror of HC10.

parent_text: Junior minister loses her seat in a by-election.
text: Not saying she deserved to lose, but she spent five years sneering at people like me, so forgive me if I'm not crying.
note: Lean N. Apophasis: denies deservingness while implying it. 'Not crying' matches 'no sympathy'. Literal coders give 3; also, losing an election is a sanction, so 'celebrates a sanction' (2) is arguable.

text: What he said was racist, full stop. He needs to understand why it hurt people and do the work.
note: Lean L. Mirror of HC14. 'Do the work' signals capacity for change, so -1. Coders outside the idiom may hear a demand for penance (+1). Score sign depends on idiom familiarity: a speaker-identity bias channel.

text: What she said about veterans was disgraceful, full stop. She needs to sit down with some of them and understand why it hurt.
note: Lean R. Mirror of HC13. Idiom is more transparent, so expect lower disagreement than HC13, which is itself a left/right asymmetry in codability.

text: Anyone still defending him after this is as bad as he is.
note: Lean N. Guilt by association. No deservingness or sanction, so 3 by the letter, yet this is how punitive targets expand to defenders (pile-on recruitment). No rule covers condemnation spreading to third parties.

text: Every time this lot open their mouths they prove they shouldn't be anywhere near power.
note: Lean N. 'Shouldn't be near power' is exclusion, which step 2 lists as a sanction, so 2. But it is an ordinary electoral judgement. Calibration example 'Remember this when you vote' is coded 1: electoral sanction is implicit there and explicit here.

parent_text: Video: shop manager shouts at a customer in a wheelchair.
text: His name is Gary Felton, he manages the Westgate branch. Just putting that out there.
note: Lean N. Fictional name. Naming a private person to invite sanction: matches 'remember the name', so 1. Yet this is the most consequential form (it mobilises a pile-on) and ranks below a mild 'she should resign' (2). Category order does not track severity. Disability context does not make it 4: the target is the manager.

parent_text: Former councillor loses appeal against his dismissal.
text: Karma's a beautiful thing. Enjoy the job centre, Darren.
note: Lean N. Celebrates a sanction, which step 2 names ('good, they deserved it'), so 2. Direct address, so spoken_about_not_to false.

text: lol he got sacked. couldn't happen to a nicer guy 😂
note: Lean N. Verbatim calibration example, which the codebook labels 1. Step 2 says celebrating a sanction is 2. Procedure and calibration table disagree; coders who learn from the table give 1, coders following the procedure give 2.

parent_text: Man filmed kicking a dog in the park.
text: I won't say what I think should happen to people like that or I'd get banned.
note: Lean N. Implied violence by paraleipsis. No sanction named, so 1, though the implied sanction is more severe than most cat 2 posts. Whether an implied wish counts towards the +3 anchor ('wishes severe harm') is unspecified.

parent_text: Bakery owner says he won't make cakes for same-sex weddings.
text: Not one more penny from me. His comments were vile.
note: Lean L. Mirror of HC22. Personal boycott of a person's business. Step 2 lists 'boycott of a person', so 2. Score anchors give +2 for a sanction demand but this is a personal choice, not a demand; +1 or +2 is a coin toss.

parent_text: Streaming channel airs a sketch mocking soldiers.
text: Cancelled my subscription. Not funding people who mock our troops.
note: Lean R. Mirror of HC21. Same act, but the target is an institution and step 2 only covers 'boycott of a person', so 3. Identical behaviour gets different categories by target type, and the split happens to fall along left/right lines here.

parent_text: MP caught claiming expenses for a second home he rents out.
text: Hope he gets everything that's coming to him.
note: Lean N. Wish for an unnamed bad outcome. 'hope they suffer' is listed under step 2, but the 1 vs 2 rule says explicit means a sanction 'is named or wished'. Vague wishes split coders between 1 and 2.

text: Muslims who celebrated the attack should be deported. All of them.
note: Lean R. Mirror of HC25. Group defined by identity plus conduct. Deportation presupposes religious or ethnic foreignness, so step 1 fires (4, mixed). Coders who treat the conduct qualifier as decisive code 2. Under current precedence the post leaves the punitive class entirely (label_pilot.py counts 4 as non-punitive).

text: Christians who voted for this bill can rot in hell. Every single one.
note: Lean L. Mirror of HC24. Same structure. Prediction: coders code majority-religion targets as 4 less often, giving 2. If the pilot shows that, step 1 is being applied by perceived group power, not by the text.

text: Typical Tory. Born rich, never worked a day, thinks the poor deserve what they get.
note: Lean L. Mirror of HC27. Party plus class: neither protected, so not 4. 'deserve' fires punitive_lexicon (and may fire deservingness), but it is the target's alleged view, not the speaker's.

text: Typical north London lefty. Lectures the rest of us on poverty from a two-million-pound house.
note: Lean R. Mirror of HC26. 1 vs 3 also live: a hypocrisy charge without deservingness could be 3.

text: Zionists have blood on their hands and should be shunned everywhere.
note: Lean L. Mirror of HC29. Political ideology or identity proxy? As written, ideology is not protected, so 2 (shunning = exclusion). Coders who read it as a proxy for Jews code 4. No rule for proxy terms.

text: Trans activists have blood on their hands and should be shunned everywhere.
note: Lean R. Mirror of HC28. 'Activists' is conduct; coders who read it as a proxy for trans people code 4. The rate of 4 should be equal across HC28 and HC29; if not, the proxy judgement is politically asymmetric.

text: Illegals who jumped the queue deserve nothing from this country. Not a penny, not a bed.
note: Lean R. Pair with HC31. Immigration status is not on the protected list (nationality is). As written: conduct (unlawful entry) plus explicit exclusion, so 2. Many coders will code 4 on the slur-like 'illegals'; dehumanising is also arguable.

text: Landlords are parasites. Every single one should have their properties seized.
note: Lean L. Pair with HC30. Occupation is not protected, so 2 with dehumanising true; seizure is 'ruin', so +3. If coders give HC30 a 4 and HC31 a 2, right-coded status-group hostility exits the punitive class while left-coded stays in, biasing H1 and H8.

text: That ref is bent. Someone check his bank account.
note: Lean N, sport. A corruption allegation supplies a moral frame, and 'check his bank account' reads as an investigation demand (3). Fans read it as banter (5); some will see contempt (1). Register is not a codebook concept.

text: You absolute muppet, you've parked across my drive again.
note: Lean N, everyday. Step 3 asks only for contempt 'because of conduct'; inconsiderate parking is conduct, so 1. Most readers would say 5. Steps 2 and 3 say 'conduct' where the construct means 'moral wrongdoing'.

text: This government is a shambles. Incompetent clowns, the lot of them.
note: Lean N. Incompetence is not moral wrongdoing, so by the construct this is 5; by step 3's wording (contempt because of conduct) it is 1. Construct and procedure diverge.

parent_text: I think rent controls would actually reduce housing supply.
text: Your argument is idiotic and so are you.
note: Lean N. Being wrong is not wrongdoing, so 5. But 'conduct' includes 'statement', so a coder can reach 1 via step 3. Score +1 inside cat 5 is permitted but shows the score is not purely punitive.

parent_text: Councillor posts beach photos while the town floods.
text: Tone-deaf muppet.
note: Lean N. Without the parent this is 5; with it, a moral frame (neglect of duty) appears, so 1. Tests whether the parent may change the category. It should, and the codebook should say so explicitly.

text: Imagine still thinking pineapple on pizza is acceptable. Unfollowing.
note: Lean N. Floor check. 'Acceptable' mimics moral vocabulary for a joke. Should be 6; an LLM primed on moral words may code 3.

text: Oh yes, very brave of him to punch down at refugees from a newspaper column. A true hero.
note: Lean L. Mirror of HC39. Intended meaning is contemptuous criticism (1, or 3 if contempt not seen). Literal meaning is praise (6). The uncertainty rule sends a low-confidence coder to the literal reading, the furthest possible label.

text: Oh yes, very brave of them to glue themselves to a motorway and make nurses late. True heroes.
note: Lean R. Mirror of HC38.

text: Another politician caught lying. I am shocked. Shocked, I tell you.
note: Lean N. Weary cynicism, no identifiable target. The no-target rule ('usually 3 or 6') gives no criterion for choosing.

parent_text: Tech billionaire's superyacht runs aground; no injuries.
text: Devastating news. Thoughts and prayers 🙏😂
note: Lean L. Mirror of HC42. Mockery of misfortune via emoji: gloating is a cat 1 signal. Score anchor +1 says 'gloat', calibration gives gloating +2. Uncodable without the parent.

parent_text: Activist's crowdfunder for legal fees closes at 4% of its target.
text: Heartbreaking. Truly a tragedy for humanity 😢😂
note: Lean R. Mirror of HC41.

text: Great idea, let's just lock up everyone who disagrees with us. What could possibly go wrong.
note: Lean N. Sarcasm opposing a punitive proposal. Intended: criticism of punitiveness (3). Literal: endorses prison (2, +2). Keyword features (punitive_lexicon fires) and literal LLM readings both pull to the wrong pole.

text: She should resign. You can't misuse public money like that and keep your job.
note: Lean N. OPEN decision 3. As written, 2 and +2: more punitive than HC10 'Absolute clown' (+1), which inverts most readers' intuitions.

text: This needs a full independent investigation, and if the allegations stand he should face the courts like anyone else.
note: Lean N. Conditional, proportionate process. Step 2 lists 'prison'; 'face the courts' is adjacent. Because the procedure stops at the first fit, step 2 is tested before the accountability boundary rule can apply.

text: Investigate him, then lock him up and throw away the key.
note: Lean N. Anchor: process plus ruin. Clear 2, +3.

text: The regulator needs to look at this. And anyone who signed it off should never sit on a board again.
note: Lean N. Process plus permanent exclusion. Score conflict: the +3 anchor names 'permanent exclusion' but calibration 'He should never work in media again' is +2.

parent_text: MP faces bullying complaints from four former staff.
text: Suspend the whip until the inquiry reports. That's how it should work for every party.
note: Lean N. A named but temporary, process-bound sanction, explicitly applied symmetrically. Step 2 fires first (exclusion), so 2, though the boundary rule's 'proportionate institutional process' clearly describes it. 'Every party' is a fairness move that would be -1 if anything.

parent_text: You lot always smear anyone who disagrees with you.
text: That's fair, we do that sometimes, and I did it to you earlier. Sorry. My actual worry is rents.
note: Lean N. Anchor: concession plus apology.

text: I've voted Conservative all my life and what was said about that Muslim councillor was disgusting. She deserves an apology.
note: Lean R speaker defending a minority-coded target. Cross-divide solidarity (-2) inside moral criticism (3). 'deserves' trips punitive_lexicon and may trip deservingness, though the outcome is good. Mention of a protected identity may pull careless coders (or keyword features) to 4.

text: Honestly, most people on the other side of this want the same things for their kids as I do. We just disagree on how to get there.
note: Lean N. Good faith to opponents with no criticism. -1 is defined as 'criticism paired with recognition', which does not apply, so -2 by elimination; coders will also give -1 or 0. No anchor for solidarity without a live conflict.

text: I was one of the people piling on him last week. I got it wrong and I've messaged him to apologise.
note: Lean N. Self-directed admission plus repair.

text: I disagree with almost everything she stands for, but the abuse she's getting is vile and she doesn't deserve any of it.
note: Lean N. Opponent defending opponent: -2. But it also condemns the abusers as 'vile', which a coder may treat as contempt for them (1, +1). Two targets with opposite stances; no rule says which target governs.

parent_text: Our striker dives in the box, gets booked, and we lose 1-0.
text: Hope he never plays for us again. Disgrace to the shirt.
note: Lean N. Wish of exclusion for conduct (simulation), so 2. Fan register leads many to read heat-of-the-moment banter (3 or 5).

text: Funny how Steve always 'forgets' when it's his round. Some people are just takers.
note: Lean N. 'Some people are just X' matches calibration 'Some people are just beyond help' (1). Shows how low-stakes the cat 1 threshold is; such posts will dominate cat 1 counts in non-political strata.

parent_text: Reality TV star apologises for racist tweets from 2014.
text: The apology's fine, but why is she still being paid to sit on that panel?
note: Lean N. Rhetorical question implying removal while setting aside the apology. No named sanction (not 2), no contempt (arguably 3). This is exactly the polite-sanction iceberg case D1 should catch, and the codebook has no rule for implied sanctions.

text: To whoever let their dog foul outside the school gates: you are a disgusting human being.
note: Lean N. Direct address to an unknown target. 1 vs 3 turns on whether 'disgusting' is anger or contempt.

text: My manager took credit for my work again. I'm so angry I could scream.
note: Lean N. Anchor for 'anger alone does not make a post punitive'.

parent_text: Singer pulls out of a charity gig to attend an awards show.
text: Good. Hope the tour flops and she has to sell the mansion.
note: Lean N. Wish of financial harm. Is 'sell the mansion' ruin (+3) or a sanction (+2)? Anchors give no severity scale for material loss.

parent_text: Runner caught cutting the course at Saturday parkrun.
text: Name and shame. Same bloke did it last month.
note: Lean N. Explicitly calls for a shaming sanction, but shaming is not on step 2's list (and Braithwaite would ask whether it is reintegrative). Coders split 1 vs 2.
